title: What spending reveals
header_line: My analysis of one book on habits. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: What do your last three months of spending say about you?
I asked what money can reveal about a person. A student said: where you spend reveals your priorities and your positive and negative habits, such as whether you are impulsive.

I said I cannot think of a better way to study a person's habits than looking at their credit card bills, and recalled the saying that history does not repeat itself, humans always do. The attribution is to be checked.
I asked: do our habits pay us interest? Do we rationalize how we spend? I needed that, I really need a new car. We can rationalize all day, but is it true to who we want to become?
A student said: negative triggers around money can be external pressure, being around certain people, and emotional catalysts before a purchase.
I asked about generational triggers. A student said: seeing how your parents handle money can turn into a pattern, or the opposite, because it left a mark on you; either way, it has an effect.

I said that people who grew up in hard times keep a preservation mode. I distinguished rich from wealthy: a rich person can afford the expensive car, house and boat; wealthy is the income that is not spent, the hidden part, having your options open with money in the bank.
Where do you see yourself in the rich and wealthy distinction?
Education, not advice. This is not financial advice.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: List your top five spends last month.
Write what each says about your priorities.
Write a trigger around money you notice.
Write what wealth means to you.

check.q: What did a student say spending reveals?
What did I ask about habits?
How did I describe being wealthy?

recap: Read your spending like a diary. Know rich from wealthy, in your own words.
